extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy, metaphysics, and comparative religion
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and applies the authorial criteria for distinguishing mysticism, asceticism, and religion from proper philosophical method; assesses moral action in relation to the denial of the will. Useful for analyzing philosophical treatments of mysticism and religious practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical method: limit to what can be proved
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosopher 'rejects all assumptions which cannot be established, and takes as his data only what can be certainly proved in the world given in external perception, in the forms of apprehension of this world, which are constitutive of our intellect, and in the consciousness of one's own self which is common to all.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophy must 'remain cosmology, and cannot become theology.' It should begin 'from without' (objective phenomena) and avoid asserting unverifiable inner intuitions. Anti-pattern: claiming positive knowledge of what is 'for ever inaccessible to all knowledge.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of mysticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Mysticism (in the widest sense) is 'every guidance to the immediate consciousness of that to which neither perception nor conception, thus in general no knowledge extends.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mystic 'starts from his inner, positive, individual experience' and finds assertions that are not communicable. Mysticism therefore indicates the inaccessible by negations and by symbolic signs; it supplements philosophical negative knowledge with inward positive claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: mystic vs philosopher (communicability and persuasion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mystic's assertions are personal and 'nothing of this is communicable except the assertions which one has to accept upon his word; consequently he cannot convince.' The philosopher 'can convince' because he uses common, objective data and reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation: prefer methods and claims that are publicly demonstrable and argumentatively persuasive. Anti-pattern: presenting private 'intellectual intuitions' as public proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning against intellectual-intuition claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosopher 'ought therefore to beware of falling into the way of the mystics, and, for example, by the assertion of intellectual intuitions or pretended immediate apprehensions of the reason, to seek to make a vain show of positive knowledge of that which is for ever inaccessible to all knowledge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not present alleged immediate apprehensions of the reason as established knowledge. Such moves are characterized as vain show and are to be avoided in sound philosophical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical acceptance of negative knowledge at limits
rubrics_metrics.description: When philosophy reaches its highest point it 'assumes a negative character, thus ends with a negation' and can speak only of what is denied; it can only indicate what is won as 'nothing' relative to our categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use negation and symbolic indication where concepts/language fail. Recognize that 'for thought this can only be expressed by negations,' and that mysticism may offer the positive supplement but is not philosophically demonstrable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of the will as the true end (moral criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral virtues are 'really not the ultimate end, but only a step towards' the denial of the will to live; 'the denial of the will to live, in consequence of the appearance of a better knowledge, is, on the other hand, salvation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral action by whether it advances the agent from assertion to denial of the will (from original sin to salvation). Moral virtues are valuable insofar as they lead to renunciation and the abolition of willing; otherwise they are intermediate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asceticism/quietism/mysticism interconnection
rubrics_metrics.description: Quietism (surrender of all volition), asceticism (intentional mortification of one's own will), and mysticism (consciousness of identity with all things) 'stand in the closest connection; so that whoever professes one of them is gradually led to accept the others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the practical signs and practices (celibacy, voluntary poverty, abstention from animal food, self-mortification, prayer at death) as expressions of this cluster. Note the cultural variations (Buddhism rejects excessive mortification; Christianity emphasizes celibacy) and that acceptance of one tendency often implies movement toward the others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs and rites indicating mystic practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Mysticism is 'indicated by symbolical signs; in temples by dim light and silence; in Brahmanism indeed by the required suspension of all thought and perception for the sake of sinking oneself profoundly in the grounds of one's own being, mentally pronouncing the mysterious Oum.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing religious or mystical practice, take ritual features (silence, dimness, suspension of thought, mantra) as intentional methods to facilitate inward immediate consciousness. These are not proof of philosophical truth but are markers of mystic technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of authenticity for mystical experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'great internal agreement, along with the firmness and certainty of their utterances' across widely different ages, countries, and religions 'proves all the more that they speak from real inward experience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cross-cultural and historical agreement and the subjective firmness of the accounts as evidence (not proof) of an inward experiential phenomenon. Recommendation: read primary mystic texts directly (e.g., Meister Eckhard, Tauler, Madame de Guion) rather than relying on second-hand reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious-historical criterion: ascetic tendency as marker of genuine Christianity
rubrics_metrics.description: The ascetic tendency (renunciation, self-denial, perfect chastity, mortification of the will) is described as 'unmistakable in the genuine and original Christianity' and as its 'summit towards which all strives upwards.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the authenticity or 'original' character of Christian teaching, consider the prominence of ascetic ideals (celibacy, virginity, contempt for marriage as concession) in patristic and early Church writings. Anti-pattern: equating later accommodation to worldly norms with original doctrine.
